doc.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: High notes on the clarinet and Dick Wellstood
summary: Rowe praises the purposefulness of his high notes; Davern says it is part of his lingua franca and Rowe cues a recording.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: No. But I have to comment on your use of high notes on the clarinet, that I’ve noticed, in my humble opinion, that they always have a purpose.

But you know like last night you hit one and it was beautiful in itself but it went even higher, it was like not the end in itself, it wasn’t like I’m going to hit this note because I know the fingering.
No. Well it was to end a tune, you know. I’d rather end a tune high than low, but also it was a C above C concert, and it happened to be the root of the chord.

Yeah, but I think it was even before that. It was in your solo and you hit this really quite high note but it wasn’t — I don’t know, I can’t even put it into words, but it was a very musical moment rather than just—
Well shouldn’t it all be musical, I mean high or low.
I mean it’s part of my lingua franca. Isn’t it? I mean, my lingua franca. You have to have a Dick Wellstood.
Oh — I’m glad you reminded me of that.
I’m going to put this on. © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-
